## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a17-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Heating</dt><dd>A line's <span class="lx-term" data-term="thermal-rating">thermal rating</span> caps its current; at a given voltage that is a limit on <span class="lx-term" data-term="apparent-power">apparent power</span> (MVA), not MW alone.</dd>
<dt>Voltage sag</dt><dd>Power drawn along a <span class="lx-term" data-term="feeder">feeder</span> lowers the voltage toward its far end; the normal band is 0.95 to 1.05 <span class="lx-term" data-term="per-unit">per unit</span>.</dd>
<dt>Hosting capacity</dt><dd>Rooftop solar that sends power back up a feeder raises its voltage; the most it can take within the limits is its <span class="lx-term" data-term="hosting-capacity">hosting capacity</span>.</dd>
<dt>Ramps</dt><dd>A plant can change its output only so fast; an hourly plan without a ramp rule can ask for more.</dd>
<dt>Inertia</dt><dd>Stored rotational energy sets how fast frequency starts to fall after a trip. Inverters can help too; how much and how fast depends on their controls, spare power and current limits.</dd>
<dt>What catches them</dt><dd>An AC check of voltage and reactive power; ramp limits checked at the plan's time step, with finer steps for changes inside the hour; and a check of the first seconds.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The five first estimates, with this lesson's numbers</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

| Check | First estimate | In this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| Apparent power | $S = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ | $\sqrt{110^2 + 50^2}$ = 120.8 MVA |
| Current in each wire | $I_\text{A} = 1000\,S_\text{MVA} \div (\sqrt{3}\,V_\text{kV})$ | 1000 × 120 ÷ (√3 × 138) = 502 A |
| Voltage at the far end | $V_\text{end} = V_\text{sub} - (R P + X Q) \div V_\text{nom}^2$ | 1.03 − (2.0 × 4.0 + 3.2 × 1.315) ÷ 155.5 = 0.951 per unit |
| Hosting capacity | $P_\text{pv} = (R P_L + X Q_L + (1.05 - V_\text{sub}) V_\text{nom}^2) \div (R - X q)$ | (2.0 × 1.0 + 3.2 × 0.33 + 0.02 × 155.5) ÷ 2.0 = 3.1 MW |
| Starting rate of change of frequency | $f_0\,\Delta P \div (2E)$ | 60 × 100 ÷ (2 × 16,000) = 0.19 Hz per second |

- **Power and wires.** $P$ in MW, $Q$ in Mvar, $S$ in MVA; $R$ and $X$ in ohms (Ω); the factor 1,000 turns kA into A.
- **Voltages.** $V_\text{nom}$ is the nominal line-to-line voltage in kV (12.47² = 155.5); $V_\text{sub}$ and $V_\text{end}$ are in per unit of it.
- **Noon symbols.** $P_L$ and $Q_L$ are the noon load's MW and Mvar; $q$ is the Mvar absorbed per MW of solar: 0 at a power factor of 1, 0.33 at 0.95.
- **Frequency symbols.** $f_0$ = 60 Hz; $\Delta P$ is the MW lost in the trip; $E$ is the stored rotational energy in MW·s (16 GW·s = 16,000 MW·s).
- **How close is the estimate?** An AC calculation of this feeder, exact for one load at its far end, gives 0.945 per unit at 4.0 MW, not 0.951: the evening limit is near 3.8 MW, not 4.1.
- **At noon it errs the other way:** the AC check finds a little more room than 3.1 MW of solar, and with absorbing inverters no voltage limit up to 8 MW.
- **The starting slope** holds only for a moment: [lesson 3](03-balancing.html) adds load relief and governors.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>What M1's DC model drops, and what replaces it</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **DC power flow** ([M1](m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html)) holds every voltage at 1.0 per unit, assumes small angle differences, and leaves out losses and reactive power.
- **An AC power flow** keeps them: non-linear equations for every voltage's size and angle, solved by iteration, for example with Newton's method ([PyPSA's documentation](https://docs.pypsa.org/latest/user-guide/power-flow/), accessed 5 November 2026).
- **The workflow.** Plan with a fast linear model, then check the plan's hours with an AC power flow and its largest trips with a dynamics study.
- **Out of this course's scope:** AC optimal power flow and dynamic simulation.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The drop through the last transformer and the service wires: the far end of the feeder stands in for a home's meter.</li>
<li>Load and solar spread along the feeder, regulators that change taps through the day, and the feeder's own heating and protection, which can bind first.</li>
<li>Moves inside the hour: real-time markets re-dispatch every five minutes, as <a href="https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/oc/2022/20220222-special/20220222-item-06-energy-market-practices-for-intermittant-resources.ashx">PJM's</a> does.</li>
<li>Load relief, governors and reserves after the first second (<a href="03-balancing.html">lesson 3</a>); inverters' current limits and control settings.</li>
<li>N−1 checks of the network after any one line fails (<a href="f06-grid-and-outages.html">F6</a>), and stability problems such as oscillations.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a17-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mw" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If every line is within its MW limit in the model, no line will overheat.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Heating follows current, and reactive power adds current: 110 MW with 50 Mvar is 120.8 MVA, over a 120 MVA rating.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="solar" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Rooftop solar can only help a feeder's voltage.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At noon, rooftop solar above about 3 MW at this feeder's far end lifts its voltage over 1.05 per unit.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spin" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Batteries cannot help in the first second after a trip, because nothing in them spins.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth: a grid-forming inverter can respond from the first instant. In the sketch, a battery assumed to give its 50 MW at once halves the starting fall after a 100 MW trip.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="hourly" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plan that balances every hour can always be run.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Without a ramp rule, M1's day asks the gas plant to climb 50 MW into 14:00, though it can change by only 40 MW an hour.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a17">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="which" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which check would catch a feeder's far end sagging below 0.95 per unit?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">An AC check of voltage and reactive power</li><li data-value="b">A ramp rule</li><li data-value="c">A check of the first seconds</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>An AC check. M1's model omits feeders, and its DC approximation does not calculate voltage-magnitude changes or reactive power.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="double" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Double the grid's stored rotational energy. What happens to the starting rate of change of frequency after the same trip?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">It doubles</li><li data-value="b">It halves</li><li data-value="c">It stays the same</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>It halves: the starting fall is f₀ × ΔP ÷ (2E), so twice the energy E gives half the fall.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card a17-practice">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Practice · about 20 minutes on your own</p>
<ol class="lx-fb-practice">
<li><p><b>Heating.</b> A 230 kV line rated 320 MVA carries 300 MW and 100 Mvar. Is it within its rating, and what current flows in each wire?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Within, barely: √(300² + 100²) = 316.2 MVA, 99% of its rating; 316.2 MVA ÷ (√3 × 230 kV) = 794 A.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Power factor.</b> What is the Ridge–Town line's power factor at 110 MW and 50 Mvar?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>110 ÷ 120.8 = 0.91.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A shorter feeder.</b> 12.47 kV, 1.5 Ω and 2.4 Ω (resistance, reactance); far end 3 MW at a power factor of 0.95; substation 1.02 per unit. Is the far end in the band, by a first estimate?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Yes. The load draws Q = P × √(1 ÷ PF² − 1) = 3 × 0.329 = 0.99 Mvar; then 1.02 − (1.5 × 3 + 2.4 × 0.99) ÷ 155.5 = 0.976 per unit.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A longer feeder.</b> Double the lesson's feeder to 16 km (4.0 Ω and 6.4 Ω), same noon load and set point. What is its hosting capacity at a power factor of 1?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 2.3 MW: (4.0 × 1.0 + 6.4 × 0.33 + 0.02 × 155.5) ÷ 4.0, less than the 3.1 MW of the 8 km feeder.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A bigger trip.</b> A 200 MW plant trips on a grid with 10 GW·s of stored rotational energy. How fast does frequency start to fall?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>60 × 200 ÷ (2 × 10,000) = 0.6 Hz per second.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A ramp.</b> Demand climbs steadily for an hour, from 100 to 210 MW of gas. The combined-cycle plant, at 100 MW, climbs 40 MW an hour; the 100 MW peaker starts at once, climbing 100 MW an hour: can they?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Yes: by the hour's end the combined-cycle plant is at 140 MW and the peaker gives 70 MW. In between, the peaker covers what the slower climb cannot, within its 100 MW an hour.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Read a claim critically.</b> A report says: “Our plan is feasible: it meets demand in every hour of the year.” What four checks would you ask about?</p><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Lines with reactive power counted; feeder voltages where rooftop solar grows; ramps at the plan's time step and below it; the first seconds after the largest trip.</p></details></li>
</ol>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>Loads can test the wires too. In July 2024, after a fault on a 230 kV line in Loudoun County, Virginia, was cleared normally, about 1,500 MW of data-center load dropped off at once (NERC).</p>
<p class="lx-hint">An hourly energy plan cannot see that.</p>
</div>

NREL/TP-5D00-77156. ANSI C84.1 ranges, Table 1, p. 4; inverters absorbing reactive power to limit voltage rise and raise hosting capacity, p. 8.</li>

<li>U.S. Department of Energy. <a href="https://www.energy.gov/eere/us-atlas-electric-distribution-system-hosting-capacity-maps">U.S. Atlas of Electric Distribution System Hosting Capacity Maps</a> (updated July 2025).</li>
```
